name: Blackburn Cathedral
text: Your train passes near Blackburn Cathedral, on the train's {side}, on a site that has had a parish church for more than a thousand years. The church was rebuilt between 1820 and 1826 and became a cathedral in 1926, when the Diocese of Blackburn was created.

name: River Blakewater
text: Your train passes near the River Blakewater, on the train's {side}, which gave Blackburn its name, meaning 'dark coloured stream'. Through the town centre it was put in a culvert during the Industrial Revolution and now runs underground, and it joins the River Darwen by Witton Country Park.

name: Pleasington Priory
text: Your train passes near Pleasington Priory, on the train's {side}, a Catholic church built between 1816 and 1819 as a thank offering by John Francis Butler, to designs by John Palmer. It is listed at Grade I, and Nikolaus Pevsner called it 'an astonishing church'.

name: Hoghton Tower
text: Your train passes near Hoghton Tower, on the train's {side}, a fortified manor house on a hilltop, built in about 1560 to 1565 for Thomas de Hoghton. King James I visited in August 1617; the house was later damaged in the Civil War and became derelict, and was rebuilt between 1862 and 1901.

name: Imperial Mill
text: Your train passes near Imperial Mill, on the train's {side}, a cotton spinning mill built in 1901 beside the Leeds and Liverpool Canal to designs by P. S. Stott. It was later taken over by the Lancashire Cotton Corporation, and production there stopped in 1980.

name: Holy Trinity Church, Blackburn
text: Your train passes near Holy Trinity Church, on the train's {side}, built between 1837 and 1846 to designs by the Lancaster architect Edmund Sharpe, with seats for 1,626 people. Lack of money held up its tower until 1853 and the planned spire was never built; it is now cared for by the Churches Conservation Trust.

name: St Gabriel's Church, Blackburn
text: Your train passes near St Gabriel's Church, on the train's {side}, built between 1932 and 1934 as the first Anglican church by the Liverpool-born architect F. X. Velarde. It is seen as a milestone in modern English church architecture, and at the time it was said to bring the style of the modern cinema into church design.

name: Whalley Abbey
text: Your train passes near the ruins of Whalley Abbey, on the train's {side}, founded when Cistercian monks moved here from Stanlow Abbey on the Mersey; Henry de Lacy laid the first stone in June 1296. After the Dissolution a country house was built on the site, now a retreat and conference house for the Diocese of Blackburn.

name: Clitheroe Castle
text: Your train passes near Clitheroe Castle, on the train's {side}, probably built by the Normans in the 12th century; its keep is the second smallest surviving stone keep in England. In 1920 the castle was sold to the people of Clitheroe as a war memorial, and it now houses a museum.

name: Gisburn Tunnel
text: Your train goes through Gisburn Tunnel, under Gisburne Park. Lord Ribblesdale wouldn't let the railway cross his grounds in case it frightened his horses, so a cut-and-cover tunnel with castellated entrances was built, and the line opened to passengers on June 1st 1880.

name: Aspden
text: Your train passes near Aspden, on the train's {side}, a small valley now called Aspen. A loop of the Leeds and Liverpool Canal bounds it on three sides, and a high railway embankment on the fourth.

name: Globe Works
text: Your train passes near the Globe Works, on the train's {side}, set up in 1853 to make machinery for Lancashire's textile industry. Its firm, Howard & Bullough, became known for looms: James Bullough, who joined in 1856, created the Lancashire Loom with William Kenworthy. What remains is now offices, the Globe Centre.

name: Accrington Town Hall
text: Your train passes near Accrington Town Hall, on the train's {side}, which opened in 1858 as the Peel Institute, an assembly hall paid for by public subscription in memory of the former Prime Minister Sir Robert Peel. It became the headquarters of the new borough in 1878, and the Accrington Pals battalion was formally raised inside it in September 1914.

name: Shuttleworth Hall
text: Your train passes near Shuttleworth Hall, on the train's {side}, a 17th-century manor house listed at Grade I, with the date 1639 over the outer door of its porch. By 1856 it was a farmhouse, and it is now two separate homes.

name: Hapton Castle
text: Your train passes near the site of Hapton Castle, on the train's {side}, at the edge of Castle Clough and now a scheduled monument. The name Hapton is thought to come from Old English words meaning the enclosure on the hill.

name: Holy Trinity Church, Burnley
text: Your train passes near the former Holy Trinity Church, on the train's {side}, built in 1835 to 1836 to designs by Lewis Vulliamy. It closed in 1990 and, after being damaged by fire, was restored and turned into flats in 1993.

name: Moorhouse's Brewery
text: Your train passes near Moorhouse's Brewery, on the train's {side}, founded by William Moorhouse in 1865 to make mineral waters and, later, low-alcohol hop bitters that were sold around the world. It first brewed cask ale in 1978.

name: River Brun
text: Your train passes near the River Brun, on the train's {side}, which is generally thought to have given Burnley its name: the meadow or clearing by the brown river. It is briefly put in a culvert under the town centre before it joins the River Calder.

name: St Peter's Church, Burnley
text: Your train passes near St Peter's Church, on the train's {side}, Burnley's parish church, on a site that had a church before 1122. The lower part of its tower, from the 15th or 16th century, is the oldest part, and from 1901 to 1977 its rectors were also the Bishops of Burnley.

name: St Mary's Church, Nelson
text: Your train passes near the former St Mary's Church, on the train's {side}, built in 1879 to designs by Waddington and Dunkerley, with its tower added between 1905 and 1908. It closed in 1989; a developer was refused permission to knock it down, and the Heritage Trust for the North West later took it on and repaired it.

name: Phoenix Foundry
text: Your train passes close to the site of Phoenix Foundry, on the train's {side}, where William Roberts and Company built many of the steam engines that drove the cotton mills of Pendle. Between 1880 and 1895 it made more than 20 mill engines of 300 to 1,000 horsepower.

name: Todmorden Unitarian Church
text: Your train passes near a Unitarian church, on the train's {side}, completed in 1869 in honour of John Fielden, a local mill owner, social reformer and Member of Parliament. It is listed at Grade I and is in the care of the Historic Chapels Trust.

name: St John the Baptist's Church, Arkholme
text: Your train passes near St John the Baptist's Church at Arkholme, on the train's {side}, which stands within the bailey of a former castle, overlooking the River Lune, with the 11th-century motte to its north-east. There has been a church here since about 1450.

name: Hincaster Tunnel
text: Your train passes near Hincaster Tunnel, on the train's {side}, which takes the Lancaster Canal through Hincaster Hill; it opened in 1819 and is lined with about four million bricks. There was no towpath through it, so horses were led over the hill on a path that is now a scheduled monument.

name: Kemp Howe
text: Your train passes Kemp Howe, a stone circle now mostly buried under the railway's embankment. It was the southern end of the Shap Avenue of standing stones, which before it was destroyed was one of the largest megalithic monuments in Europe.

name: St Mary's Church, Wreay
text: Your train passes near St Mary's Church, Wreay, on the train's {side}, designed by Sara Losh and built between 1840 and 1842. It is the earliest known example in Britain of a revival of Lombard architecture, and its churchyard holds a copy of the Bewcastle Cross.

name: Carlisle Castle
text: Your train passes near Carlisle Castle, on the train's {side}, first built in 1092 in the reign of William II and rebuilt in stone in 1122. During the Jacobite Rising of 1745 to 1746 it became the last English fortress to undergo a siege.

name: Tullie House
text: Your train passes near Tullie House, on the train's {side}, a Jacobean mansion that Carlisle Corporation opened as a museum in 1893, when it also held a library, an art school and a technical school. The building is listed at Grade I.

name: Carlisle Citadel
text: Your train passes near the Citadel, on the train's {side}, a fortress built for Henry VIII and finished in 1541. It became a prison in 1611, and its two towers were turned into law courts to designs by Thomas Telford and Sir Robert Smirke in 1812 and 1822.

name: Cardew Lodge
text: Your train passes near Cardew Lodge, on the train's {side}, a hunting lodge built for Major-General William Henry Lowther after he retired from the Bengal Army in the late 1870s. Its single-storey gabled wings recall an Indian bungalow.

name: Wigton School
text: Your train passes close to Brookfield, on the train's {side}, home of a Quaker boarding school that the Society of Friends opened in 1815 and moved here in 1826, into Georgian buildings designed by a London architect. Its motto was 'We seek the truth'.

name: Bullgill
text: Your train passes Bullgill, on the train's {side}, a hamlet that grew up as a mining community; the Ellen Pit coal mine was sunk in 1859. Bullgill had its own station, which closed to passengers on March 7th 1960.

name: Milefortlet 25
text: Your train passes the site of Milefortlet 25, the southernmost known of the small Roman forts that, with watchtowers, carried the defences of Hadrian's Wall along the Cumbrian coast. Nothing of it can be seen now: the site is built over.

name: Derwent Park
text: Your train passes near Derwent Park, on the train's {side}, the home of Workington Town rugby league club, opened in 1956. A motorcycle speedway track runs round the pitch, and the record crowd, 17,741, came for a Challenge Cup match against Wigan in 1965.

name: St Michael's Church, Workington
text: Your train passes near St Michael's Church, on the train's {side}, the parish church of Workington. Its oldest part dates from about 1150, and there is evidence of a seventh-century monastery on the same site.

name: Lowca
text: Your train passes close to Lowca, on the train's {side}. On August 16th 1915 the German submarine U-24 fired 55 shells at a coke and toluene works near the village, doing little damage; it was probably the first time Britain had been bombarded by a submarine.

name: St James' Church, Whitehaven
text: Your train passes near St James' Church, on the train's {side}, built in 1752 to 1753 on high ground overlooking the town and listed at Grade I. Its design has been attributed to Carlisle Spedding, agent and mining engineer to Sir James Lowther.

name: Carlisle Turkish baths
text: Your train passes near Carlisle's Turkish baths, on the train's {side}, built in 1908 to 1909 beside the city's swimming pool of 1884. They were used until November 2022 and keep their original tiling and faience, of unusually good quality.

name: Cumwhinton
text: Your train passes near Cumwhinton, on the train's {side}, a village that began as a hamlet by the middle of the 12th century. It was first called Cumquintina, a name believed to come from Saint Quentin.

name: Eden Gorge
text: Your train runs along Eden Gorge, on the train's {side}, a Site of Special Scientific Interest covering five kilometres of the River Eden's valley, with cliffs 30 metres high where the river has cut through New Red Sandstone. Its woods include sessile oak, birch and hazel.
